subject: trouble with modeling evolution of a latent trait

messages.author: 9d61e7b0823c1527
messages.subject: trouble with modeling evolution of a latent trait
parts:
Hi all,

I am working on estimating latent national public opinion ("theta") for 126 countries over 25 years using around 3000 observed nationally-aggregated responses to 33 survey questions drawn from across these countries and years. 

The model, below, is mostly working fine, except for the autoregressive / dynamic component. I treat this as a random walk, so theta[t,j] ~ normal(theta[t-1,j], sigma_theta), for t time periods and j countries. 

The trouble is with sigma_theta, the evolution parameter. The sampled values hover around a reasonable value (0.03) with Rhats in the 1.3-1.4 range. But it 
never converges even as the rest of the model settles down pretty quickly (within say 1000 iterations and 4 chains). 

I suppose I could just throw 5000 iterations at the problem, but I suspect there is some issue with identification.

I began with a half-cauchy(0, 2) prior but am now using a half-normal(0, 0.5), which appears marginally better.

Thanks in advance for any comments or suggestions


data{
  int<lower=1> N;               // number of national survey opinions
  int<lower=1> J;               // number of countries
  int<lower=1> K;           // number of items by project 
  int<lower=1> T;           // number of years
  int<lower=1,upper=J> jj[N];   // country j for opinion n
  int<lower=1,upper=K> kk[N];   // item-project k for opinion n
  int<lower=1,upper=T> tt[N];   // year t for opinion n
  real xsq[N];   // vector of survey opinions, 0-1, squared
}

parameters{
  matrix[T,J] theta;                // matrix of T by J latent traits
  vector<lower=0>[K] sigma_eps; // K item-project-specific residual error variances 
  real<lower=0> sigma_theta;        // opinion evolution error variance
  vector[K-1] alpha_est;                // estimated item-project location parameters
  real<lower=0> sigma_alpha;     // item-project-level error variance 
  real mu_alpha;             // expectation of item-project location pars
}

transformed parameters{
  real x_hat[N];                 // fitted values
  vector<lower=0>[N] sigma_eps_kk; // N-expanded residual error variances
  vector[K] alpha;                     // item-project location parameters
  alpha[1] <- .575; // constrain 1st loc. par. to observed mean
  alpha[2:K] <- alpha_est[1:(K-1)];     // map item location params to alpha vector
  sigma_eps_kk <- sigma_eps[kk];
  for (i in 1:N) // fitted values model
    x_hat[i] <- alpha[kk[i]] + theta[tt[i],jj[i]];
}
 
model{
  theta[1] ~ normal(0, 0.5); // latent trait evolution model 
  to_vector(theta[2:T]) ~ normal(to_vector(theta[1:(T-1)]), sigma_theta); 
  xsq ~ normal(x_hat, sigma_eps_kk); // response model
  alpha_est ~ normal(mu_alpha, sigma_alpha);
  sigma_theta ~ normal(0, 0.5);
  sigma_alpha ~ cauchy(0, 2);
  sigma_eps ~ cauchy(0, 2);
  mu_alpha ~ normal(0, 2);
}

generated quantities {
  vector[N] x_pred;
  for (i in 1:N)         // simulate fitted data to check model
    x_pred[i] <- normal_rng(x_hat[i], sigma_eps_kk[i]);
}

parts:
Ok. That's a start. Is there high autocorrelation? If so, try reparameterizing (non-centered teparameterization)? Or simulating from known values and hitting to that to see if the model is working correctly. 

If the estimates are different across chains, there's something else going on.


Daniel

parts:
You might want to try a non-centered parameterization
for alpha:
> x_hat[i] <- alpha[kk[i]] + theta[tt[i],jj[i]];

> alpha[1] <- .575; // constrain 1st loc. par. to observed mean
> alpha[2:K] <- alpha_est[1:(K-1)]; // map item location params to alpha vector
> alpha_est ~ normal(mu_alpha, sigma_alpha);

> theta[1] ~ normal(0, 0.5); // latent trait evolution model
> to_vector(theta[2:T]) ~ normal(to_vector(theta[1:(T-1)]), sigma_theta);

That'd be:

alpha_est ~ normal(0, 1);
alpha[1] = 0.575;
alpha[2:K] = mu_alpha + sigma_alpha * alpha_est;

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] trouble with modeling evolution of a latent trait
parts: You can also non-center the thetas in the same way.
> to_vector(theta[2:T]) ~ normal(to_vector(theta[1:(T-1)]), sigma_theta);

theta_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
theta[2:T] = theta[1:(T - 1)] + sigma_theta * theta_raw;

- Bob

> On Jul 25, 2016, at 12:51 PM, Christopher Claassen <chris.c...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks Bob and Daniel.
>
> I did implement the non-centered parameterization for alpha after I made the first post (although the alphas were converging OK). I didn't think to do it for sigma_theta however. I guess I had figured the non-centered parameterization works only for hierarchical coefficients (such as alpha).
>
> Would I do this by using a non-centered parameterization for the thetas, or directly for sigma_theta, their evolution parameter?
>
>
>
>
> On Monday, 25 July 2016 17:04:37 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> You might want to try a non-centered parameterization
> for alpha:
>
> > x_hat[i] <- alpha[kk[i]] + theta[tt[i],jj[i]];
> > alpha[1] <- .575; // constrain 1st loc. par. to observed mean
> > alpha[2:K] <- alpha_est[1:(K-1)]; // map item location params to alpha vector
> > alpha_est ~ normal(mu_alpha, sigma_alpha);
> > theta[1] ~ normal(0, 0.5); // latent trait evolution model
> > to_vector(theta[2:T]) ~ normal(to_vector(theta[1:(T-1)]), sigma_theta);
>
> That'd be:
>
> alpha_est ~ normal(0, 1);
> alpha[1] = 0.575;
> alpha[2:K] = mu_alpha + sigma_alpha * alpha_est;
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Jul 25, 2016, at 10:32 AM, Christopher Claassen <chris.c...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Daniel,
> >
> > R-hat remains at around 1.3-1.4 despite 2000 iterations.
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > On Monday, 25 July 2016 14:54:42 UTC+1, Daniel Lee wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > What do you mean when you say that sigma_theta never converges? Mind describing what diagnostics you're looking at to say that?
> >
> >
> > Daniel
> >
> >
> > On Mon, Jul 25, 2016 at 6:03 AM, Christopher Claassen <chris.c...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi all,
> >
> > I am working on estimating latent national public opinion ("theta") for 126 countries over 25 years using around 3000 observed nationally-aggregated responses to 33 survey questions drawn from across these countries and years.
> >
> > The model, below, is mostly working fine, except for the autoregressive / dynamic component. I treat this as a random walk, so theta[t,j] ~ normal(theta[t-1,j], sigma_theta), for t time periods and j countries.
> >
> > The trouble is with sigma_theta, the evolution parameter. The sampled values hover around a reasonable value (0.03) with Rhats in the 1.3-1.4 range. But it
> > never converges even as the rest of the model settles down pretty quickly (within say 1000 iterations and 4 chains).
> >
> > I suppose I could just throw 5000 iterations at the problem, but I suspect there is some issue with identification.
> >
> > I began with a half-cauchy(0, 2) prior but am now using a half-normal(0, 0.5), which appears marginally better.
> >
> > Thanks in advance for any comments or suggestions
> >
> >

> > int<lower=1> N; // number of national survey opinions
> > int<lower=1> J; // number of countries
> > int<lower=1> K; // number of items by project

> > int<lower=1,upper=T> tt[N]; // year t for opinion n
> > real xsq[N]; // vector of survey opinions, 0-1, squared
> > }
> >
> > parameters{

> > }
> >
> > transformed parameters{

> > alpha[2:K] <- alpha_est[1:(K-1)]; // map item location params to alpha vector
> > sigma_eps_kk <- sigma_eps[kk];
> > for (i in 1:N) // fitted values model
> > x_hat[i] <- alpha[kk[i]] + theta[tt[i],jj[i]];
> > }
> >
> > model{
> > theta[1] ~ normal(0, 0.5); // latent trait evolution model
> > to_vector(theta[2:T]) ~ normal(to_vector(theta[1:(T-1)]), sigma_theta);
> > xsq ~ normal(x_hat, sigma_eps_kk); // response model
> > alpha_est ~ normal(mu_alpha, sigma_alpha);
> > sigma_theta ~ normal(0, 0.5);
> > sigma_alpha ~ cauchy(0, 2);
> > sigma_eps ~ cauchy(0, 2);
> > mu_alpha ~ normal(0, 2);
> > }
> >
> > generated quantities {
> > vector[N] x_pred;
> > for (i in 1:N) // simulate fitted data to check model

> > }
> >
